lessons.title: Choosing the Right Sunflower Variety for Your Region
lessons.body: Choosing the right sunflower variety is the first step to a successful harvest. In Africa, varieties are bred for different climates: some tolerate drought, others resist diseases common in humid areas. You must match the variety to your local rainfall, temperature, and soil. For dry regions like northern Nigeria or Kenya's semi-arid areas, choose short-season varieties such as 'PAN 7351' or 'Sungold' that mature in 85-100 days. These need less water and escape late-season drought. In wetter areas like Uganda or Malawi, select taller, longer-season varieties like 'Record' or 'Hybrid 66' that can reach 120 days but yield more oil. Always check with your local agricultural extension officer or research station for recommended varieties in your district. They often have trial data showing which varieties perform best in your agro-ecological zone. Avoid planting varieties that are not adapted to your area, even if they are cheap or donated. A wrong variety can fail completely. Also consider your market: if you sell to oil processors, high-oil hybrids like 'Hysun 33' are best; for bird feed or local consumption, larger-seeded open-pollinated varieties like 'Fedha' work well. Seed labels should state the variety name, maturity days, and disease resistance. If you save seed from hybrid varieties, the next generation will not be true to type and yields will drop. So buy fresh hybrid seed each season. For open-pollinated varieties, you can save seed but must select the best plants and store properly. Remember, variety choice affects everything: planting date, spacing, fertiliser needs, and pest management. Spend time researching before you buy. Visit a nearby farmer who grows sunflower and ask what works. Your choice today determines your harvest tomorrow.

lessons.title: Hybrid vs Open-Pollinated Varieties
lessons.body: Sunflower varieties come in two main types: hybrids and open-pollinated (OP). Understanding the difference helps you decide which to plant. Hybrids are created by crossing two parent lines. They give higher yields, more uniform plants, and better disease resistance. For example, hybrid 'PAN 7049' can yield 2.5 tonnes per hectare, while OP 'Local' may yield only 1 tonne. Hybrids also have stronger stalks and uniform maturity, making harvest easier. But hybrid seed is more expensive and must be bought every season. If you save seed from hybrids, the next crop will be a mix of weak and strong plants, reducing yield by 30-50%. Open-pollinated varieties are naturally pollinated and stable. You can save seed from your best plants and replant next season. They are cheaper and good for low-input farming. Examples include 'Fedha', 'Sungold', and many local landraces. However, OP varieties often yield less and vary in height and maturity. They may also be more susceptible to diseases like rust and downy mildew. In Africa, many smallholders use OP varieties because they cannot afford hybrid seed each year. But if you can access hybrid seed through subsidy or credit, it often pays off. Consider your goal: if you sell to a processor demanding uniform seed, hybrids are better. If you grow for home use and want to save seed, OP is practical. You can also plant both: a hybrid for cash and an OP for seed. Always buy certified seed from reputable agrodealers. Avoid grain from the market, as it may be treated with chemicals or be a non-adapted variety. Check the label for germination percentage and purity. With good management, both types can be profitable. Choose based on your budget, market, and willingness to buy seed annually.

lessons.title: Seed Quality, Certification, and Treatment
lessons.body: Good seed is the foundation of a good crop. Poor-quality seed leads to weak plants, low yields, and wasted money. Always buy certified seed from a licensed agrodealer or seed company. Certified seed has a blue or green label with information: variety name, lot number, germination percentage, purity, and date of testing. Germination should be at least 85% for sunflower. If it is lower, you may need to plant more seeds per hole. Check the seed physically: it should be uniform in size, colour, and shape, with no cracks, mould, or insect holes. Shriveled or discoloured seeds are dead or diseased. You can do a simple germination test at home: count 100 seeds, place them between moist cloths or paper towels, keep them warm and moist for 7-10 days, then count how many sprout. If fewer than 80 sprout, buy new seed. Seed treatment is common. Many certified seeds are coated with fungicides and insecticides to protect against soil-borne diseases and early pests. The coating may be pink, green, or blue. Never eat treated seed or feed it to animals. If you buy untreated seed, you can treat it yourself with thiram or captan before planting, following label instructions. Wear gloves and a mask. Store seed in a cool, dry place in a sealed container. Avoid storing near fertiliser or chemicals. Moisture and heat kill seed quickly. In humid areas, add a desiccant like silica gel. Use seed within one year. If you save seed from open-pollinated varieties, select heads from the healthiest, highest-yielding plants. Dry them thoroughly, thresh gently, and store in airtight jars. Always label your saved seed with the variety and date. By investing in quality seed and proper treatment, you give your sunflower crop the best start.

lessons.title: Planting Date Determination and Soil Temperature
lessons.body: Planting at the right time is critical for sunflower. If you plant too early, cold soil and frost can kill seedlings. If you plant too late, the crop may suffer from drought, heat, or pest outbreaks. The key is soil temperature. Sunflower seeds germinate best when soil temperature at 5 cm depth is at least 8-10Â°C and stable. In most African regions, this occurs after the first reliable rains. For example, in Zimbabwe's highveld, plant from mid-November to early December. In Kenya's Rift Valley, plant with the long rains in March-April. In West Africa's savanna, plant in June-July after the onset of steady rains. You can measure soil temperature with a simple soil thermometer, available at agrodealers. Insert it 5 cm deep in the morning for three consecutive days. If the average is above 10Â°C, you can plant. Another sign: when you can walk barefoot on the soil comfortably, it is warm enough. Avoid planting in dry soil hoping for rain; seeds may rot or be eaten by ants. Also avoid planting right after a heavy downpour, as soil may crust and prevent emergence. Sunflower is photoperiod-sensitive: some varieties need short days to flower. So choose a planting date that gives the crop enough growing degree days before the onset of frost or extreme heat. In areas with two rainy seasons, the first season is usually better for sunflower because of longer days and less disease. If you plant late, choose a short-season variety. Keep records of planting dates and weather each year to refine your timing. Talk to neighbours and extension officers about the best planting window in your area. A difference of one week can mean the difference between a bumper harvest and a failed crop.

lessons.title: Planting Methods: Row Spacing, Plant Density, and Depth
lessons.body: How you plant sunflower affects yield, weed control, and harvest. Sunflower is usually planted in rows to allow easy weeding and spraying. The recommended spacing depends on variety and rainfall. For hybrid varieties in good rainfall areas, use 75 cm between rows and 25-30 cm between plants. This gives about 44,000 to 53,000 plants per hectare. In drier areas, increase spacing to 90 cm by 30 cm to reduce competition for water, giving about 37,000 plants per hectare. For open-pollinated varieties, wider spacing of 90 cm by 40 cm is common. Plant density matters: too dense and plants compete for light, water, and nutrients, producing small heads. Too sparse and you waste land and get lower total yield. Aim for the recommended density for your variety and environment. Planting depth should be 3-5 cm. Deeper planting (more than 6 cm) can prevent emergence, especially in heavy soils. Shallower planting (less than 2 cm) may lead to drying out or bird damage. Plant 2-3 seeds per hole and thin to one plant per station 10-14 days after emergence. Thinning reduces competition and allows uniform growth. You can plant manually using a hoe or dibble stick, or use a seed drill for large areas. If using a drill, calibrate it to drop the right number of seeds. After planting, firm the soil lightly to ensure good seed-soil contact. Avoid planting on slopes where seeds may wash away. In dry areas, plant in furrows to capture water. Always plant in straight rows to make weeding and harvesting easier. Mark row ends with stakes. With correct spacing and depth, your sunflower will have room to grow strong and produce heavy heads.

lessons.title: Seedbed Preparation and Establishment Techniques
lessons.body: A good seedbed gives sunflower seedlings a strong start. Sunflower has a deep taproot, so soil should be loose and well-drained to at least 30 cm depth. Start preparing land early, before the rains. Clear bushes and previous crop residues. Plough to a depth of 20-30 cm, then harrow to break clods and level the soil. If you use conservation agriculture, you can plant directly into residues with a ripper or jab planter, but ensure the soil is not compacted. In small plots, use a hand hoe to prepare a fine tilth. Avoid over-tilling, which can cause crusting and erosion. Add organic matter like compost or manure (2-4 tonnes per hectare) during land preparation to improve soil fertility and water holding. If soil is acidic (pH below 5.5), apply agricultural lime at 1-2 tonnes per hectare, based on soil test results. Sunflower tolerates a range of soils but prefers pH 6.0-7.5. After planting, establishment techniques ensure good germination. If rains are erratic, you may need to water lightly after planting. Keep the seedbed weed-free, especially in the first 4-6 weeks. Weeds compete for nutrients and water. Use a hoe or hand weeding, or apply a pre-emergence herbicide like pendimethalin before emergence. Be careful with herbicides; sunflower is sensitive to some chemicals. Check the label. If crusting occurs after heavy rain, break the crust gently with a rake to help seedlings emerge. Protect seedlings from birds, rodents, and insects. Birds can pull up seedlings; use scarecrows or reflective tape. Cutworms and termites can be controlled with seed treatment or bait. Thin to one plant per station when plants are 10-15 cm tall. A well-prepared seedbed and careful establishment set the stage for a healthy, high-yielding sunflower crop.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Seed Selection and Planting for Sunflower Farming in Africa

Sunflower is one of Africa's most commercially versatile oilseed crops. It matures in 90â130 days, tolerates marginal soils better than maize, and feeds directly into edible oil, animal feed, and confectionery value chains. For the African agribusiness operator, the margin between profit and loss is decided long before the first leaf emerges â at seed selection and planting. A poorly chosen variety or a badly timed planting date can cut yield by 40â60%, destroying the return on every input naira, shilling, or rand spent. This reference consolidates the technical decisions that determine establishment success across African agro-ecological zones.

1. Choosing the Right Sunflower Variety for Your Region

Variety choice must be driven by three commercial questions: What is my end market? What is my rainfall regime? What disease pressure exists in my area?

  • Oil market: Choose high-oil hybrids (40â50% oil content). Buyers pay premiums for oil content above 42%.
  • Confectionery/birdseed market: Choose large-seeded open-pollinated or specialised confectionery hybrids with striped or black-and-white seed coats.
  • Short-season zones (e.g., Sudan, northern Nigeria, Ethiopia's lowlands): Select early-maturing varieties (90â105 days).
  • High-rainfall/humid zones (e.g., Uganda, Tanzania's southern highlands): Select varieties with strong tolerance to Sclerotinia head rot and rust.

Africa's dominant sunflower-producing countries â Tanzania, South Africa, Uganda, Zambia, and Nigeria â each have national variety lists maintained by their research councils. Always verify that a variety is registered and recommended for your specific agro-ecological zone before purchase.

2. Hybrid vs Open-Pollinated Varieties

This is the single most consequential commercial decision for a sunflower enterprise.

Table 1: Hybrid vs Open-Pollinated Sunflower â Commercial Comparison
Parameter Hybrid Varieties Open-Pollinated Varieties (OPVs)
Yield potential (rainfed, Africa) 1.8â3.0 t/ha 0.8â1.5 t/ha
Oil content 40â50% 32â40%
Seed cost per hectare USD 25â60 USD 8â20
Seed saving / replanting Not viable (yield collapses 30â50% in F2) Viable for 2â3 generations with selection
Uniformity of maturity High â single-pass harvest Low â staggered maturity, multiple passes
Disease resistance Often bred-in (downy mildew, rust) Variable, generally weaker
Best fit Commercial oil production, contract farming Smallholder, low-input, seed-security systems

Source: FAO (2010). Sunflower: Agronomy and Production; and IITA Sunflower Production Guide for Sub-Saharan Africa.

Business verdict: If you are selling to an oil processor on contract, hybrids are non-negotiable â the oil content alone justifies the seed cost. If you are a smallholder in a low-input system with no guaranteed market, a certified OPV such as Record or Fedha may deliver better risk-adjusted returns.

3. Seed Quality, Certification, and Treatment

Counterfeit and expired seed is a major cause of crop failure across Africa. Protect your investment with these checks:

  • Certification: Buy only from registered agro-dealers. Insist on a seed certification label from the national seed authority (e.g., NASC in Nigeria, TOSCI in Tanzania, KEPHIS in Kenya, SANSOR in South Africa).
  • Germination rate: Minimum 85% for commercial planting. Request a germination test certificate.
  • Seed treatment: Treated seed (fungicide + insecticide coating) protects against damping-off and soil-borne pests. Untreated seed is cheaper but riskier in moist soils.
  • Storage: Seed must be stored below 12% moisture. Never buy seed from open sacks exposed to humid air.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â TREATED SEED

Treated sunflower seed is coated with fungicides and insecticides that are toxic to humans and animals. Never eat treated seed, never feed it to livestock, and never use it for oil extraction. Store treated seed away from food and out of reach of children. Wear gloves when handling, and wash hands thoroughly after planting. Dispose of empty seed bags by burning or burying â never reuse them for food storage.

4. Planting Date Determination and Soil Temperature

Sunflower is temperature-sensitive at establishment. The crop will not germinate reliably below 8Â°C soil temperature, and frost at emergence is fatal. The optimal window is when soil temperature at 5 cm depth is consistently 10â12Â°C and rising.

African regional planting windows:

  • Southern Africa (South Africa, Zambia, Zimbabwe): Plant NovemberâDecember with summer rains.
  • East Africa (Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda): Plant at the onset of the long rains (MarchâApril) or short rains (OctoberâNovember) depending on zone.
  • West Africa (Nigeria, Ghana): Plant JuneâJuly with the main rains; avoid late planting that pushes grain fill into dry season.
  • Sahel (Sudan, northern Nigeria): Plant with the first reliable rains (JuneâJuly), using early-maturing varieties.

5. Planting Methods: Row Spacing, Plant Density, and Depth

Sunflower is a "self-thinning" crop â get the density right at planting and you avoid costly thinning labour. The table below gives commercially validated recommendations.

Table 2: Recommended Planting Parameters for Sunflower by Production System
Parameter Rainfed Smallholder Rainfed Commercial Irrigated Commercial
Row spacing (cm) 60â75 75â90 75
Plant spacing within row (cm) 25â30 20â25 18â22
Target plant population (plants/ha) 40,000â55,000 55,000â65,000 65,000â75,000
Sowing depth (cm) 3â5 3â5 2.5â4
Seed rate (kg/ha) 4â6 5â7 6â8
Expected yield (t/ha) 0.8â1.5 1.8â2.5 2.5â3.5

Source: FAO (2010) Sunflower: Agronomy and Production; ARC-South Africa (2019) Sunflower Production Guidelines; IITA (2018) Sunflower Production Guide for Sub-Saharan Africa.

Key rules:

  • Depth: Never plant deeper than 5 cm. Deep planting exhausts the seed's stored energy before the seedling reaches light. In light sandy soils, 4â5 cm is safe; in heavy clay, 3 cm is safer.
  • Density: Higher density increases oil yield per hectare but reduces individual head size. For confectionery markets, reduce density to 35,000â45,000 plants/ha to maximise seed size.
  • Spacing uniformity: Gaps and doubles cost yield. Calibrate your planter or use a measured string line for manual planting.

6. Seedbed Preparation and Establishment Techniques

Sunflower has a deep taproot but a relatively weak seedling. A well-prepared seedbed is essential for uniform emergence.

  • Primary tillage: Plough to 20â25 cm to break compaction and incorporate crop residues. In conservation agriculture systems, direct-seed into a killed cover crop.
  • Secondary tillage: Harrow to produce a fine, level seedbed. Cloddy seedbeds cause uneven emergence and poor herbicide efficacy.
  • Soil pH: Target 6.0â7.5. Sunflower tolerates slight acidity but is sensitive to aluminium toxicity below pH 5.5. Apply lime 3â6 months before planting if needed.
  • Fertiliser at planting: Apply 200â300 kg/ha of compound fertiliser (e.g., NPK 7:14:7 or 12:24:12) placed 5 cm below and 5 cm to the side of the seed â never in direct contact with seed.
  • Weed control: Sunflower is a poor competitor early. Apply pre-emergence herbicide at planting or plan for two manual weedings at 3 and 6 weeks after emergence.
  • Establishment check: Aim for 90% of target population surviving to 3 weeks. Replant if establishment falls below 60%.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. â Confirm variety is registered for your agro-ecological zone and matches your end market (oil vs confectionery).
  2. â Verify seed certification label, germination rate (â¥85%), and expiry date before purchase.
  3. â Check soil temperature at 5 cm depth is â¥10Â°C and rising before planting.
  4. â Calibrate planter or measure spacing for target population of 40,000â65,000 plants/ha.
  5. â Set sowing depth at 3â5 cm â never deeper.
  6. â Apply starter fertiliser 5 cm below and beside the seed, never in contact with it.
  7. â Handle treated seed with gloves; store away from food and feed.
  8. â Inspect establishment at 3 weeks; replant if survival is below 60%.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Sunflower: Agronomy and Production (free PDF)
  • IITA â Sunflower Production Guide for Sub-Saharan Africa
  • ARC-South Africa â Sunflower Production Guidelines
  • KEPHIS Kenya â Seed Certification and Variety List
  • NASC Nigeria â National Seed Certification Standards

This module is part of the Rise Africa Skills programme. All recommendations should be validated against your local extension service and current input prices before committing capital.

quiz.q: Which factor is most important when choosing a sunflower variety for your region?
options: A) The colour of the seed
B) The local climate and rainfall pattern
C) The price of the seed
D) The size of the seed
quiz.explanation: Varieties must match local climate and rainfall to perform well.

quiz.q: Which of these is a short-season sunflower variety suitable for dry areas?
quiz.explanation: PAN 7351 matures in 85-100 days and tolerates drought.

quiz.q: What should you do if you want to save seed for next season?
options: A) Save seed from hybrid varieties
B) Save seed from open-pollinated varieties
C) Save seed from any variety
D) Buy new seed every season
quiz.explanation: Open-pollinated varieties can be saved and replanted true to type.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of hybrid sunflower varieties?
options: B) They can be saved for next season
C) They give higher yields and uniform plants
quiz.explanation: Hybrids typically yield more and are more uniform than open-pollinated types.

quiz.q: If you save seed from a hybrid variety, what happens?
options: A) The next crop will be identical
B) The next crop will have lower yield and variable plants
C) The next crop will be more resistant to disease
D) The next crop will mature earlier
quiz.explanation: Hybrid seed saved will not be true to type, causing yield loss.

quiz.q: What is the minimum germination percentage recommended for sunflower seed?
quiz.explanation: Certified sunflower seed should have at least 85% germination.

quiz.q: How can you test seed germination at home?
options: A) Soak seeds in water overnight
B) Place seeds between moist cloths for 7-10 days
C) Plant seeds in the field and count
D) Look at the seed colour
quiz.explanation: A simple germination test uses moist cloths to see how many seeds sprout.

quiz.q: What does a pink or green coating on sunflower seed indicate?
options: B) The seed has been treated with fungicide or insecticide
C) The seed is genetically modified
D) The seed is ready to eat
quiz.explanation: Seed treatment coatings protect against pests and diseases.

quiz.q: How should you store sunflower seed?
options: A) In a warm, humid place
B) In a cool, dry place in sealed containers
quiz.explanation: Cool, dry storage maintains seed viability.

quiz.q: What is the ideal soil temperature for planting sunflower?
quiz.explanation: Sunflower seeds germinate best when soil is at least 8-10Â°C.

quiz.q: In Zimbabwe's highveld, when is the recommended planting time for sunflower?
quiz.explanation: Planting with the first reliable rains in November-December is ideal.

quiz.q: What tool can you use to measure soil temperature?
quiz.explanation: A soil thermometer inserted 5 cm deep gives accurate readings.

quiz.q: What is a sign that soil is warm enough for planting?
options: A) You can walk barefoot comfortably
quiz.explanation: Comfortable barefoot walking indicates warm soil.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid planting sunflower too late?
options: B) Crop may suffer drought and heat
C) Plants will be too tall
D) Heads will be too small
quiz.explanation: Late planting exposes the crop to drought and heat stress.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for hybrid sunflower in good rainfall areas?
quiz.explanation: 75 cm between rows and 25-30 cm between plants is standard.

quiz.q: What is the ideal planting depth for sunflower seed?
quiz.explanation: Planting 3-5 cm deep ensures good emergence.

quiz.q: How many seeds should you plant per hole?
quiz.explanation: Plant 2-3 seeds and thin to one plant later.

quiz.q: When should you thin sunflower seedlings?
quiz.explanation: Thinning at 10-14 days reduces competition.

quiz.q: What is the target plant population for hybrid sunflower in good rainfall areas?
quiz.explanation: 44,000-53,000 plants per hectare is optimal for hybrids.

quiz.q: Why is it important to firm the soil after planting?
options: B) To ensure good seed-soil contact
quiz.explanation: Firming improves seed-soil contact for germination.

quiz.q: What is the recommended ploughing depth for sunflower seedbed preparation?
quiz.explanation: Sunflower has a deep taproot, so plough to 20-30 cm.

quiz.q: What is the ideal soil pH for sunflower?
quiz.explanation: Sunflower prefers slightly acidic to neutral soil pH.

quiz.q: How much organic manure should be applied per hectare during land preparation?
quiz.explanation: 2-4 tonnes per hectare improves soil fertility and structure.

quiz.q: What should you do if the soil is acidic (pH below 5.5)?
quiz.explanation: Lime raises soil pH to the optimal range.

quiz.q: Why is it important to control weeds early in sunflower?
options: B) Weeds compete for nutrients and water
quiz.explanation: Early weed control prevents competition during critical growth stages.

quiz.q: Which pre-emergence herbicide can be used in sunflower?
quiz.explanation: Pendimethalin is commonly used pre-emergence in sunflower.

quiz.q: What should you do if soil crusts after heavy rain?
options: B) Break the crust gently with a rake
quiz.explanation: Breaking the crust helps seedlings emerge.

quiz.q: How can you protect sunflower seedlings from birds?
options: A) Use scarecrows or reflective tape
quiz.explanation: Scarecrows and reflective tape deter birds.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of planting sunflower in rows?
options: B) It makes weeding and spraying easier
quiz.explanation: Rows allow efficient mechanical or manual operations.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of using certified seed?
options: B) It has known germination and purity
C) It can be saved for many years
quiz.explanation: Certified seed guarantees quality parameters.
